title: Absalom, my son (2 Samuel 18:33)
hookLine: David's rebel son dies and the king weeps: would I had died for you
last: I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.

lines: A WAR AGAINST HIS OWN SON.
cards: Two runners are coming across the plain. The king sits between the two gates of the city, waiting, and a watchman on the roof of the gate calls down what he sees. The battle is over, a battle against David's own son.
Absalom, praised in all Israel for his looks, had stolen the people's hearts, declared himself king, and driven his father out of Jerusalem. Now the armies have met in a forest.
The first runner arrives: the king's enemies are defeated. David asks only one question: is the young man Absalom safe?

teach.h: DEAL GENTLY WITH THE YOUNG MAN.
teach.b: Before the battle, David gave one order, in front of the whole army: "Deal gently for my sake with the young man, even with Absalom." It wasn't obeyed.
Absalom rode his mule under the thick branches of a great oak, his head caught fast, and he was left hanging between heaven and earth.

Joab, the general, who had heard the king's order, thrust three darts into him, and Joab's armor-bearers finished it. A second runner comes. The runner says it gently: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is.

In the King James Bible: "And the king was much moved, and went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept: and as he went, thus he said, O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!"
Read it aloud and it barely holds together.

It's a man climbing to a room over a gate, saying the same few words over and over. Some readers hear in it the shadow of Nathan's words: trouble rising from David's own house. None of that stops the grief.
The text counts the cost too: the soldiers come back into the city quietly, like people ashamed, because their victory had turned into mourning.

teach.h: WOULD GOD I HAD DIED FOR THEE.
teach.b: One Christian reading is a parent's love that outlasts betrayal and would trade places with the child who wronged him.
Some Christians hear an echo of their teaching about Jesus: that God did what David could only wish, and died for those who had turned away.

how: Some Christians turn to David's lament for Absalom when speaking of a parent's grief, and some hear in it a picture of God's love for those who have turned away.

games.q: you're David. your son led a rebellion against you, and your army has won. the runner tells you your son is dead. what do you do?
o: thank your men for the victory.
go up to the room over the gate and weep for him.
say he got what he deserved.
games.why: he goes up to the chamber over the gate weeping: "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee."

practice: Some of us know a mother or father who has lost a child, through death, or estrangement, or a road the child chose, and some of us are that parent; if someone comes to mind, let them come, gently. Don't try to say anything wise.
If you pray, pray for them in silence or in your own words; if you don't, simply hold them with care.

wordCard.voice: Absalom. David's son, who rebelled against him and died in the forest, and whom the king mourned: would God I had died for thee.

orig.note: Hebrew: my son. David's cry over Absalom repeats it (2 Samuel 18:33).

carryVoice: Your line: my son, my son. Some grief is only a name, said again. Go gently.
